title: First tests: score, boilerplate, notify, culture probes
description: Repo has zero tests. stdlib unittest only - the README promises no dependencies, so pytest is off the table. Highest value first: score.dealbreaker and score.score, the boilerplate stripper, notify.unsent plus the notified table, culture.assess probes.

title: Strip per-company boilerplate before scoring
description: Top measured accuracy defect. GitLab ships 1,483 identical chars on all 219 of its postings, so every role inherits the company's entire stack: a Staff EMEA-only field role scored skills 40.0/40 while a genuine backend role scored 56.7 and was never emailed. culture.boilerplate(rows) already computes the longest common prefix but nothing consumes it. Strip it before score.score() reads terms. Evidence: eval/out/cards.md, regenerate with eval/blindset.py.

title: Daily requirements digest: what the top matches actually ask for
description:
Mentor needs to know every day what the highest-scoring postings actually require,
so lessons and interview prep track the live market instead of a snapshot. Today
that answer took a hand-rolled sqlite query and a throwaway python histogram.

Build `./jobhunt.py requirements [--top N] [--since DATE] [--show TERM]`.

WHAT IT EMITS (out/requirements-digest.md)
1. Requirement clusters across the top N scored postings (default 25), grouped by
   requirement shape, not by company.
2. Every requirement line cites the postings it came from (company + title). Same
   principle as the scorer: a wrong line must be a line you can fix, not a black
   box you have to trust.
3. A delta against the previous run - requirements that entered, dropped, and the
   companies that moved in or out of the top N. A daily digest that does not say
   what changed will not get read daily.

DO NOT RANK BY RAW TERM FREQUENCY
A term count over a corpus measures how verbose the postings are, not how much
the requirement matters. In today's top 30, "agent" appeared 126 times - 61 of
them from GitLab alone, 35 from Replit. Rank by DISTINCT POSTINGS mentioning the
requirement, weighted by that posting's score. Raw count may appear as a column;
it must not drive the order.

VERIFY BY READING, NOT BY COUNTING
A phrase match over human prose is a hypothesis until someone reads the sentences
it matched. `--show TERM` prints the matched sentences with their source posting
so a claimed requirement can be spot-checked in one command.

DELIVERY
Runs daily. Writes the file, then drops an fps-services notice for mentor
containing the delta only - three lines, facts not context. The digest itself
lives in the file.

title: Show eligibility flags in list and digest output
description: gate.flags() already computes region_locked / degree_hard / equivalency_ok / level_mismatch and gate.py is wired into 'jobhunt gate'. Confirm the flags reach 'jobhunt list' and the email digest - a flag nobody sees is a silent filter by another name. Alex has no completed degree and applies on experience, so degree language is a flag he reads, never a filter that hides a job.

title: GitHub Actions on push and pull request
description: Run the stdlib unittest suite plus the stdlib-only import gate. Keep it dependency-free and fast. Mirror the workflow written for arscholtes/fps.

title: Close 'ships often' with a GitHub-org and blog-feed source
description: Culture is a separate axis, shown not summed into the fit total. 'Ships often' is the highest-weighted term (5) and is unknown for all 13 companies because culture.py works corpus-only. Add an unauthenticated GitHub-org API probe plus blog/changelog feeds. Do NOT fold culture into the score.

title: exclude_titles misses new grad / early career / junior
description:
profile.toml exclude_titles covers intern/principal/staff/manager/director/sales/
recruiter but not new-grad language, so early-career postings rank near the top of
the shortlist: notion "Software Engineer, New Grad (Dec 2026)" scores 92.0 (3rd
overall), "Software Engineer, Early Career (AI)" 81.7, "Software Engineer, Early
Career" 73.2.

They score high because they are genuine keyword matches - the stack and the
interests line up. Nothing in the model knows they are closed to a candidate with
six years of experience.

Add "new grad", "early career", "junior", "apprentice" to exclude_titles. Check
whether "associate" belongs there too: it currently pulls in non-engineering
postings (Credit Risk Associate, Customer Experience Associate) that survive only
because they score low, not because anything rejected them.

title: Resume tailoring per posting
description: resume.py already generates variants from a canonical resume.toml, so the artifact is not a blocker. Tailoring is choosing and adjusting the variant for one posting. Single-column, no tables, no sidebars - two-column layouts scrambled in 7 of 8 ATS parsers tested and tables dropped in 5 of 8.

title: Application drafting
description: Draft the application from the tailored resume plus what the culture axis knows about the company. Nothing here contacts an employer: drafting and sending stay separate, deliberate human steps.
